conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the surgery team members. You’re here today for your scheduled pancreas and kidney transplant, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve been waiting for this call for months. Is everything set for surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry, but I have some news. The donor organs were evaluated and unfortunately weren’t suitable for transplant. They didn’t meet the safety or function criteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I was really hoping this would happen. Does that mean I’m not getting the transplant at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not today. You’re still fully listed and active for transplant. This just means we have to wait for another donor match. It’s disappointing, but not uncommon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I guess I just feel let down. I’ve been doing everything right—my PD, my meds, my diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You absolutely have. Your labs look stable—creatinine is high as expected, but no signs of infection or acute issues. Your chest X-ray also looks clear, which is good for surgical clearance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that DNR status on file since last time. Does that affect anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s actually something we discussed with the team. Since you were admitted for transplant, we temporarily reversed your DNR status for the perioperative period, just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. But since there’s no surgery, does that mean my DNR is back in place?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, since no procedure is happening, your current wishes stand. The transplant clinic will follow up with you about the MOLST form and your code status.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I just want to be clear about what happens next.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. You’ll go home today. You should continue your peritoneal dialysis as usual and take all your regular medications, including insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on domperidone before—can I restart that? It helps with my gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve added domperidone to your discharge list—10 mg three times a day before meals. It’s safe with your current meds and should help with fullness and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. And if I get sick or something changes, I should call the transplant clinic, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Any hospitalization, illness, or even insurance changes—let them know. It could affect your listing status.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. So no surgery today, but I’m still on the list and just waiting for the next call.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. We know it’s frustrating, but your spot hasn’t changed. We’ll keep supporting you until the right match comes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for explaining everything. I was nervous coming in, but I feel better knowing what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You should be able to go home in the next hour or so.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I monitor my blood sugar more closely now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep checking as usual. Your HbA1c is 6.4%, which is good control. Just stick with your glargine and sliding scale as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my PD—no changes there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No changes. Continue your peritoneal dialysis exactly as you do at home. If you notice any signs of infection around the catheter, call your nephrologist right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for walking me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll be in touch if anything changes. Take care, and we’ll see you when the next opportunity comes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be ready. Thank you.
